choose.prompt: Do you know what time the library closes tonight?
options: Yes, I read that book last week.
I think it's open until ten.
No, I don't have a library card.
It's on the second floor.
choose.why: Gefragt ist nach der Uhrzeit – nur diese Antwort nennt eine Zeit.

choose.prompt: Would you like to get lunch after class?
options: No, the class is in Room 12.
I had a class this morning.
Sure, I'm starving.
It was a really good lunch.
choose.why: Einladung → Zusage. starving = sehr hungrig.

choose.prompt: Where did you park your car?
options: It's a blue car.
Yes, I parked it.
About twenty minutes ago, I think.
Right behind the science building.
choose.why: Where → Ortsangabe.

choose.prompt: How was your weekend?
options: Pretty relaxing, thanks.
It's on Saturday.
I'll be away next weekend.
Two days, I think.
choose.why: How was …? → Bewertung des vergangenen Wochenendes.

choose.prompt: Can you lend me a pen?
options: No, I didn't send it.
Here, you can keep it.
Yes, it's a long essay.
I wrote it yesterday.
choose.why: Bitte um einen Stift → Stift wird gegeben.

choose.prompt: Is this seat taken?
options: The seats are blue.
Yes, I took the class last year.
No, go ahead.
It's very comfortable.
choose.why: Is this seat taken? = Ist hier frei? → No, go ahead.

choose.prompt: Have you finished reading the article for tomorrow?
options: Yes, I wrote the article.
It was published in a journal.
I'll read it to you tomorrow.
Almost. I just have a few pages left.
choose.why: Frage nach dem Stand → fast fertig.

choose.prompt: Why is the bus so late today?
options: There's construction on Main Street.
It usually comes every ten minutes.
I take the bus every day.
Yes, it's very late.
choose.why: Why → Grund (Baustelle).

choose.prompt: Didn't you say you were going to the career fair?
options: Yes, I said it to the professor.
I was, but my shift got moved.
The fair was held in the gym last year.
I'm planning to apply for that job.
choose.why: Indirekt: Plan geändert, weil die Schicht verlegt wurde.

choose.prompt: I can't believe how long this line is.
options: The line is on the next page.
I can lend you a longer one if you really need it.
Tell me about it. We've been here for twenty minutes.
I believe it's correct.
choose.why: Tell me about it = Das kannst du laut sagen (Zustimmung).

choose.prompt: Do you want me to save you a seat at the lecture?
options: The lecture was about economics.
I saved all my notes on my laptop.
No, I don't have any money left this month.
That would be great. I'm running a bit late.
choose.why: save a seat = Platz freihalten; die anderen spielen mit „save“ (speichern, sparen).

choose.prompt: Has anyone seen the remote for the projector?
options: Check the drawer under the desk.
I've never been to that room.
Yes, I saw that movie.
The projector is brand new.
choose.why: Indirekte Hilfe: Hinweis, wo sie sein könnte.

choose.prompt: I heard the professor is giving us an extra week for the paper.
options: She teaches on Mondays and Wednesdays.
Really? That's a relief.
I'd like to read it again.
The paper is ten pages long.
choose.why: Reaktion auf eine gute Nachricht: relief = Erleichterung.

choose.prompt: You're not still working on that lab report, are you?
options: The lab is on the third floor.
No, I've never worked in a lab like that before.
I'm afraid so. The data took forever to analyze.
The report has ten pages.
choose.why: I'm afraid so = leider ja; Grund folgt.

choose.prompt: Why don't we split the cost of the textbook?
options: The textbook costs about eighty dollars.
I don't know why it's so expensive.
I split it into three chapters.
Good idea. We can take turns using it.
choose.why: Why don't we …? ist ein Vorschlag, keine Frage nach dem Grund.

choose.prompt: Would you mind proofreading my cover letter?
options: Not at all. Send it over.
I don't mind the weather.
Yes, I'd love to write one.
I covered that topic in class.
choose.why: Would you mind …? → Not at all = gern (ich habe nichts dagegen).

choose.prompt: Weren't you supposed to meet with your advisor today?
options: I'm supposed to graduate in May.
She had to reschedule for Thursday.
I've had the same advisor for two years.
My advisor teaches chemistry.
choose.why: Indirekt: Das Treffen wurde verschoben.

choose.prompt: The printer in the computer lab is out of paper again.
options: I printed my essay yesterday.
The lab closes at nine.
I'll let the front desk know.
Paper is cheaper online.
choose.why: Problem gemeldet → Lösung anbieten.

choose.prompt: I could have sworn the meeting was at three.
options: It lasted about three hours.
I swear I'll be there at three.
The meeting room has three windows.
So could I, but the email says two.
choose.why: I could have sworn = ich war mir ganz sicher; So could I = ich auch.

choose.prompt: You might want to double-check those figures before you submit the report.
options: Good point. I rushed through the last section.
I'll check out a book later.
The figures are in the appendix.
I submitted my application for the program last week.
choose.why: Höflicher Rat (You might want to …) → Zustimmung mit Begründung.

choose.prompt: I'm thinking of dropping statistics this semester.
options: I dropped my phone yesterday.
Are you sure? You'd have to take it eventually anyway.
This semester ends in December.
Statistics show that most students pass the course easily.
choose.why: drop a course = einen Kurs abwählen; die Antwort hinterfragt die Entscheidung.

choose.prompt: Do you happen to know if the gym is open on holidays?
options: It happened last year as well.
I usually work out on weekends.
I'm not sure, but there's a schedule posted at the entrance.
Happy holidays to you and your whole family as well.
choose.why: Nicht wissen, aber Hinweis auf eine Informationsquelle geben.

choose.prompt: That presentation went better than I expected.
options: I expect to finish it by Friday.
It's better to present in the morning.
The presentation is next week.
You certainly didn't look nervous.
choose.why: Reaktion auf eine Aussage über die Vergangenheit mit passendem Kommentar.

choose.prompt: If you're heading to the café, could you grab me a coffee?
options: Sure. The usual?
The coffee machine was fixed yesterday.
The café has new chairs.
I grabbed the wrong bag.
choose.why: grab sb a coffee = jemandem einen Kaffee mitbringen; The usual? = wie immer?

choose.prompt: I don't suppose you've had a chance to look at my draft yet?
options: I suppose the draft is due soon.
Actually, I read it last night. It's really strong.
I haven't drafted anything for my own class yet.
There's a chance of rain later.
choose.why: I don't suppose … = höfliche, zurückhaltende Frage; Actually = doch.

choose.prompt: Isn't it about time we started on the group project?
options: The group has four members.
We started the course in September.
Definitely. How about Monday after class?
It's about three o'clock.
choose.why: Isn't it about time …? = Wir sollten langsam anfangen → Terminvorschlag.

choose.prompt: What time does the next train leave?
options: I took the train yesterday.
From platform two, I think.
It's a very long train.
In about ten minutes.
choose.why: What time → Zeitangabe.

choose.prompt: Do you want to sit inside or outside?
options: Outside, if it's not too cold.
I sat there the last time we came.
Yes, I do.
The inside is new.
choose.why: Entweder-oder-Frage → eine der Optionen wählen, nicht Yes/No.

choose.prompt: Who's teaching the history class this term?
options: It's on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
A new professor, I think. Dr. Lewis.
History started in the morning.
I'm not taking any math classes.
choose.why: Who → Person.

choose.prompt: Could you turn the music down a little?
options: Yes, it's my favorite song.
I'll turn left at the corner.
Oh, sorry. Is this better?
The music starts at eight.
choose.why: Bitte → der Bitte nachkommen.

choose.prompt: How long have you lived in this city?
options: It's a really big city.
I'm leaving next week.
Near the university.
About three years now.
choose.why: How long → Zeitdauer.

choose.prompt: Are you going to the party on Saturday?
options: I'd like to, but I have to work.
It was a great party.
On Saturday at seven.
Yes, I went there last week.
choose.why: Indirekte Absage mit Grund.

choose.prompt: Haven't you already handed in the assignment?
options: I handed out flyers yesterday.
Not yet. I'm still checking the references.
Yes, I'll hand it in tomorrow.
The assignment was easier last year, I think.
choose.why: Negativ formulierte Frage: „Not yet“ = noch nicht; „Yes … tomorrow“ widerspricht sich.

choose.prompt: Why don't you join us for the hike this weekend?
options: The hike is about ten kilometers.
Because I joined the club last year.
I'd love to. What time are you leaving?
I don't know why they left.
choose.why: Why don't you …? = Einladung, keine Frage nach dem Grund.

choose.prompt: I can't find my notes from last week's lecture.
options: I found the lecture hall easily.
The lecture starts next week.
My notes are very long.
You can borrow mine if you want.
choose.why: Problem → Hilfe anbieten.

choose.prompt: Is it okay if I bring a friend to the study group?
options: Sure, the more the merrier.
I studied with friends in high school.
Okay, I'll bring the books.
The group meets in the library.
choose.why: the more the merrier = je mehr, desto besser (Zustimmung).

choose.prompt: Didn't the professor say the exam would be open-book?
options: She's a very good professor.
Only for the second part, I think.
The exam room is closed.
I opened the book this morning.
choose.why: Präzisierende Antwort auf eine Rückfrage.

choose.prompt: You look exhausted. Late night?
options: No, I'm not late at all.
I'll be there tonight.
Yeah, I was up finishing my report.
It gets dark early these days.
choose.why: Late night? = Lange aufgeblieben? → Bestätigung mit Grund.

choose.prompt: I was under the impression the deadline had been pushed back.
options: The impression was very positive.
I pushed the door, but it was locked.
The deadline is printed on the back.
It was, but only for the graduate students.
choose.why: under the impression = dachte; pushed back = verschoben.

choose.prompt: You wouldn't happen to have a spare charger, would you?
options: I might. What kind of phone do you have?
No, I don't charge for that.
My phone is fully charged.
I happened to see him yesterday.
choose.why: Sehr höfliche, indirekte Bitte → Gegenfrage, um helfen zu können.

choose.prompt: If I were you, I'd ask for an extension.
options: Yes, you were right about the extension cord.
I might, but I'd hate to fall even further behind.
The extension is on the second floor.
I asked him yesterday where you were.
choose.why: Ratschlag → abwägende Reaktion; die anderen spielen mit „extension“.

choose.prompt: It's a shame the concert was canceled.
options: I'll cancel my order for the new speakers tomorrow.
The tickets are still on sale.
Tell me about it. I'd been looking forward to it for weeks.
Yes, it was a great concert.
choose.why: Tell me about it = volle Zustimmung.

choose.prompt: Remind me why we decided to take the scenic route?
options: We decided to take a photo.
The route is about fifty miles from here, I believe.
I'll remind you tomorrow.
Because you said the highway would be packed.
choose.why: Remind me why … = Warum noch mal …? → Grund.

choose.prompt: Don't tell me you've already finished the whole novel.
options: I couldn't put it down.
I've never read that author.
The novel has three hundred pages.
I won't tell anyone.
choose.why: Don't tell me … drückt Erstaunen aus; couldn't put it down = konnte nicht aufhören.

lines.text: Hi, I'd like to renew these two books, please.
Sure. Can I see your student ID?
Here you go. Oh, and is it possible to renew them online next time?
Yes. Just log in to the library website and click on My Account. You can renew each book up to three times.
Great, that'll save me a trip.

questions.q: What does the woman want to do?
options: Get a new student ID
Return some books
Buy a book
Renew two library books
questions.why: „I'd like to renew these two books.“

questions.q: What does the man tell the woman?
options: She can renew books online.
She needs to create a new account.
She must come to the library to renew books.
She can renew a book only once.
questions.why: Über „My Account“ online verlängern, bis zu dreimal.

lines.text: Do you want to go grocery shopping this afternoon?
I can't. I have to work until six.
Okay. Do you need anything? I can pick it up for you.
Could you get some milk and bread? I'll pay you back tonight.
No problem.

questions.q: Why can't the woman go shopping?
options: She is feeling sick.
She has to work.
The store is closed.
She already went this morning.
questions.why: „I have to work until six.“

questions.q: What will the man probably do?
options: Lend the woman some money
Cook dinner for the woman
Buy milk and bread for the woman
Wait until six to go shopping
questions.why: Er bietet an, etwas mitzubringen; sie bittet um Milch und Brot.

lines.text: Professor Kim, do you have a minute? It's about the research paper.
Of course, Daniel. What's on your mind?
I've found plenty of sources on renewable energy, but my topic feels too broad. I'm not sure where to focus.
That's a common problem. Why not pick one country and look at how its energy policy has changed over the last ten years?
That makes sense. Germany might be interesting. I've read a lot about their solar programs.
Good choice. Just make sure you use at least two academic journals, not only news articles.

questions.q: What is the man's problem?
options: He missed the deadline.
He can't find enough sources.
He doesn't understand solar energy.
His topic is too general.
questions.why: „my topic feels too broad“.

questions.q: What does the professor remind him to do?
options: Include articles from academic journals
Avoid writing about Germany
Use only news articles
Write about at least two countries
questions.why: „use at least two academic journals, not only news articles“.

lines.text: Hi, I submitted a maintenance request last week, but nobody has come to fix my heater yet.
I'm sorry about that. Let me check. It looks like your request was sent to the wrong building.
Oh no. It's been really cold at night.
I'll mark it as urgent and send it to the right team now. Someone should be there by tomorrow afternoon. In the meantime, you can pick up a portable heater at the front desk.
That would help a lot. Thanks.

questions.q: Why hasn't the heater been fixed yet?
options: A replacement part had to be ordered.
The request was sent to the wrong building.
The woman forgot to submit a request.
The repair team was too busy.
questions.why: „your request was sent to the wrong building“.

questions.q: What does the man suggest the woman do?
options: Move to another room
Wait until next week
Borrow a portable heater
Submit a new request online
questions.why: „you can pick up a portable heater at the front desk“.

lines.text: Are you ready for our presentation tomorrow?
Mostly. I finished my slides, but I still have to practice my part.
Want to do a run-through tonight? We could book a study room.
I'd love to, but I promised to help my brother move. How about early tomorrow, before class?
Hmm. I'm not really a morning person. But okay, let's meet at eight.

questions.q: Why can't the man practice tonight?
options: He has a class tonight.
He hasn't finished his slides.
All the study rooms are booked.
He promised to help his brother.
questions.why: „I promised to help my brother move.“

questions.q: What does the woman imply?
options: She doesn't like early meetings but will agree to one.
She thinks they don't need to practice.
She would rather practice alone.
She can't meet before class because of her schedule.
questions.why: not a morning person = kein Frühaufsteher; trotzdem „okay“.

lines.text: So, did you hear back from the consulting firm?
I did. They offered me the internship. The thing is, the bank I interviewed with last week might make an offer too, and they pay considerably more.
Did the bank give you a timeline?
Only that they'd decide soon. Meanwhile, the consulting firm wants an answer by Friday.
Well, a bird in the hand. Unless you'd honestly prefer the bank, I wouldn't risk losing a sure thing.
That's what I'm afraid of. Although the consulting work does sound more interesting, to be honest.

questions.q: What is the woman's dilemma?
options: Whether to ask the consulting firm for a considerably higher salary
Whether to accept one offer before hearing from another employer
Which of two offers pays more
Whether to cancel an interview
questions.why: Die Beratung will bis Freitag eine Antwort, die Bank hat noch nicht entschieden.

questions.q: What does the man mean when he says "a bird in the hand"?
options: She should accept both internships.
She should ask the bank to make its decision faster.
A certain opportunity is better than an uncertain one.
Consulting work is more interesting.
questions.why: Sprichwort: Lieber den Spatz in der Hand …

lines.text: Can I talk to you about the lab report? I noticed the discussion section is still empty.
Right. I've been swamped with midterms. I was going to get to it this weekend.
The thing is, it's due Monday morning, and I'd like time to read it over before we submit. Last time we lost points because the sections didn't match.
Fair enough. How about I send you a draft by Saturday noon?
That works. And if you get stuck on the error analysis, just let me know. I've got my notes from the review session.

questions.q: Why is the woman concerned?
options: The man made mistakes in the data.
She missed the review session.
The report is already later than the professor allowed.
She wants time to check the report before it is due.
questions.why: Sie will es vor der Abgabe gegenlesen; letztes Mal gab es Punktabzug.

questions.q: What does the woman offer to do?
options: Share her notes if the man needs help
Meet the man on Monday morning
Ask the professor for an extension
Write the discussion section herself
questions.why: „I've got my notes from the review session.“

lines.text: Excuse me, do you know how the washing machines work?
Sure. You pay with your student card. Just tap it here and choose the program.
How long does it take?
About forty minutes. The dryers take another hour, so don't wait too late at night.

questions.q: How do students pay for the machines?
options: At the front desk
With their student card
Online
With coins
questions.why: „You pay with your student card.“

questions.q: What does the man suggest?
options: Washing clothes on weekends
Using a different machine
Not starting laundry too late
Drying clothes outside
questions.why: „don't wait too late at night“.

lines.text: Hi, can I get a large coffee, please?
Sure. Would you like milk or sugar?
Just milk, thanks. Oh, and do you have anything without gluten?
Yes, the banana bread is gluten-free. It's very popular.
Great, I'll take a piece.

questions.q: What does the man order to drink?
options: A small tea
A hot chocolate
A coffee with sugar
A large coffee with milk
questions.why: „a large coffee … Just milk“.

questions.q: Why does the man ask about gluten?
options: He is looking for food without gluten.
He wants to bake bread.
He works at the café.
He wants the most popular cake.
questions.why: Er fragt nach etwas Glutenfreiem und nimmt das Bananenbrot.

lines.text: Hi, I'm thinking about studying abroad next year, but I'm worried about the cost.
That's a common concern. Many of our exchange programs let you pay your normal tuition here, so the cost isn't much higher than staying home.
Really? What about housing and flights?
Those you'd pay yourself, but there are travel grants. The application deadline is in March, and you'll need a short essay and a recommendation from a professor.
Okay, I'd better start asking a professor now, then.

questions.q: What is the woman's main concern?
options: Missing her friends
How expensive studying abroad will be
Which country to choose
Whether her language skills are good enough
questions.why: „I'm worried about the cost.“

questions.q: What will the woman probably do next?
options: Pay her tuition
Book a flight
Ask a professor for a recommendation
Contact the exchange university
questions.why: „I'd better start asking a professor now.“

lines.text: Did you end up applying for the research assistant position in Dr. Hale's lab?
I did, but I'm having second thoughts. It's twelve hours a week, and with my course load, I'm not sure I can keep up.
Twelve hours is a lot. Still, it'd look great on your grad school applications.
That's exactly why I applied. I guess I could drop my elective. It doesn't count toward my major anyway.
That seems like a reasonable trade-off, if the position works out.

questions.q: Why is the woman having second thoughts?
options: The lab is located too far from campus.
The pay is too low.
She doesn't like Dr. Hale.
She is worried she won't have enough time.
questions.why: Zwölf Stunden pro Woche plus volles Kursprogramm.

questions.q: What does the woman consider doing?
options: Dropping a course that is not required for her major
Asking to work fewer than twelve hours a week
Applying to a different lab
Postponing graduate school
questions.why: Das Wahlfach zählt nicht für ihr Hauptfach.

lines.text: Hey, are you using your camera this weekend? I'm going to my cousin's wedding, and my phone's camera isn't great.
I'm not, but it's not exactly the easiest camera to figure out. Have you used one like it before?
Not really. How hard can it be?
Well, the automatic mode is fine, but the battery drains fast. I'd take the spare one, and maybe practice a bit tomorrow so you're not figuring it out during the ceremony.
Good idea. Could you show me the basics tonight?
Sure. Swing by after dinner.

questions.q: What is the man's concern?
options: He needs the camera himself this weekend.
The woman may have trouble using the camera.
The wedding is too far away.
The camera might get damaged.
questions.why: „not exactly the easiest camera to figure out“.

questions.q: What does the man recommend?
options: Using only the manual settings for better photos
Buying a new camera
Bringing an extra battery and practicing in advance
Using her phone instead
questions.why: Ersatzakku mitnehmen und vorher üben.

announcement.text: Attention, students. The cafeteria in the Student Center will close early today, at 3 p.m., because of a staff training session. Dinner will be served as usual in the North Dining Hall from 5 to 8 p.m. We're sorry for any inconvenience.

questions.q: What is the announcement mainly about?
options: A change in dinner prices
A cafeteria closing early
A training course for students
A new dining hall opening
questions.why: Die Cafeteria schließt heute früher.

questions.q: Where can students eat dinner today?
options: Nowhere on campus
In the staff room
In the North Dining Hall
In the Student Center
questions.why: „Dinner will be served as usual in the North Dining Hall.“

announcement.text: Good morning, everyone. Today's field trip to the science museum will leave from the main entrance at nine thirty, not nine o'clock as planned. Please bring your student ID for free entry, and remember that lunch is not provided, so pack a snack or bring some money.

questions.q: What has changed?
options: The entrance fee
The date of the trip
The destination
The departure time

questions.q: What should students bring?
options: Their student ID
A packed lunch for the whole group
Their textbooks
A museum ticket
questions.why: „Please bring your student ID for free entry.“

announcement.text: Hello, this is an announcement for all residents of Maple Hall. The fire alarm system will be tested tomorrow between 10 a.m. and noon. You do not need to leave the building during the test. However, if the alarm sounds at any other time, it is a real emergency, and you must exit immediately using the nearest stairway.

questions.q: What will happen tomorrow?
options: New stairways will be built.
The fire alarm system will be tested.
Residents will attend a safety meeting.
The building will be evacuated.
questions.why: Test der Brandmeldeanlage zwischen 10 und 12 Uhr.

questions.q: What should residents do if they hear the alarm in the afternoon?
options: Take the elevator to the ground floor
Wait for further instructions
Leave the building immediately
Ignore it because it is a test
questions.why: Außerhalb des Testfensters ist es ein echter Notfall.

announcement.text: Welcome to the Riverside Art Museum. Please note that the second-floor gallery is currently closed while we install our new photography exhibition, which opens next Saturday. In the meantime, visitors can enjoy a free guided tour of our sculpture garden, starting every hour at the information desk. Photography without flash is permitted in all open areas.

questions.q: Why is the second-floor gallery closed?
options: It is reserved for a private event.
It is being repaired.
The sculptures are being cleaned.
A new exhibition is being set up.
questions.why: „while we install our new photography exhibition“.

questions.q: What is true about taking photos?
options: It is allowed without a flash.
It is not allowed anywhere.
It costs extra.
It is allowed only on guided tours.
questions.why: „Photography without flash is permitted“.

announcement.text: This is a reminder that the Economics Department's guest lecture, The Future of Remote Work, has been moved from Room 210 to the larger auditorium in Hayes Hall because of high interest. The talk begins at 4 p.m. Students who attend can earn one point of extra credit in Economics 101 by submitting a one-page summary by Friday.

questions.q: Why has the lecture been moved?
options: The time of the lecture has changed.
Many people want to attend.
The speaker asked for a larger room.
Room 210 is being renovated.
questions.why: „because of high interest“.

questions.q: How can students earn extra credit?
options: By registering online
By asking a question during the talk
By writing a short summary of the talk
By arriving early
questions.why: „submitting a one-page summary by Friday“.

announcement.text: Good afternoon. This is a message from the Office of the Registrar. Due to an unexpected technical issue with the online registration system, the registration period for spring courses has been extended by forty-eight hours and will now close on Thursday at 5 p.m. Students who encountered error messages while enrolling are advised to verify their schedules, as some selections may not have been saved. Course waitlists remain unaffected.

questions.q: Why has the registration period been extended?
options: The office will be closed for two days.
Too few students have registered.
More courses have been added.
A technical problem affected the online system.
questions.why: „Due to an unexpected technical issue“.

questions.q: What are some students advised to do?
options: Check whether their course choices were saved
Register again for all their courses
Contact their professors directly
Join a course waitlist
questions.why: „advised to verify their schedules, as some selections may not have been saved“.

announcement.text: Attention, passengers. Due to signal maintenance between Central Station and Harbor Point, Blue Line trains are running every twenty minutes rather than every eight this weekend. Passengers traveling to the airport are encouraged to allow additional time or to use the express shuttle bus, which departs from Platform 3. Weekly passes will be honored on the shuttle at no additional charge.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the announcement?
options: To advertise a new airport bus
To inform passengers about reduced train service
To explain upcoming changes to ticket prices
To announce new train routes
questions.why: Züge fahren nur alle 20 statt alle 8 Minuten.

questions.q: What is indicated about the shuttle bus?
options: It costs more than taking the train to the airport.
It only goes to Harbor Point.
Passengers with weekly passes can ride it at no extra cost.
It runs every eight minutes.
questions.why: „Weekly passes will be honored … at no additional charge.“

announcement.text: Hello, students. The bookstore will have a sale this Friday and Saturday. All T-shirts and sweatshirts will be twenty percent off. Textbooks are not part of the sale. The store will be open from nine in the morning until six in the evening on both days.

questions.q: What is on sale?
options: Everything in the store
Textbooks
Notebooks
Clothing
questions.why: T-Shirts und Sweatshirts; Lehrbücher nicht.

questions.q: When is the sale?
options: On Friday and Saturday
Every weekend this month
Next week

talk.title: Why Leaves Change Color
talk.text: Today I want to explain why leaves change color in the fall. Leaves are green during spring and summer because they contain a lot of chlorophyll. Chlorophyll is the chemical that plants use to turn sunlight into food. But leaves also contain other colors, like yellow and orange. We just can't see them in summer because there is so much green. In the fall, the days get shorter and colder. Trees stop making chlorophyll, and the green color slowly disappears. That's when the yellow and orange colors become visible. Some trees, like maples, also make a new red color in the fall. Scientists think this red color may protect the leaves from too much sunlight while the tree takes back nutrients before the leaves drop.

talk.title: The First Bicycles
talk.text: Let's look at the history of the bicycle. The first bicycle-like machine was built in Germany in 1817. It was made of wood and had no pedals. Riders sat on it and pushed themselves along with their feet. It was called a running machine. About fifty years later, pedals were added to the front wheel. These bicycles were faster, but they were also very uncomfortable. People called them boneshakers, because the roads were rough and the wheels were made of iron. Later, some bicycles had a huge front wheel and a tiny back wheel. A bigger wheel meant more speed, but riders often fell. Finally, in the 1880s, the safety bicycle appeared. It had two wheels of the same size and a chain connected to the back wheel, very similar to the bikes we ride today.

talk.title: Desire Paths
talk.text: Have you ever noticed a narrow dirt path cutting across a lawn, even though a paved sidewalk goes around it? Urban planners call these desire paths. They form when enough people decide that the official route is inconvenient and take a shortcut instead. For a long time, many planners saw desire paths as a nuisance. They put up fences or signs to keep people on the sidewalks. More recently, though, some designers have started treating these paths as valuable information. After all, a desire path shows exactly where people actually want to walk. Some universities have even used this idea when designing new campuses. Instead of paving walkways right away, they plant grass everywhere and wait a few months. Then they pave the paths that students have worn into the ground. The result is a network of walkways that matches how people really move around the campus.

talk.title: The Tragedy of the Commons
talk.text: In economics, there's an idea called the tragedy of the commons. Imagine a pasture that's open to all the farmers in a village. Each farmer benefits from adding one more cow to the field, because they get the milk and the profit. But the cost, the grass that the extra cow eats, is shared by everyone. So each farmer has a reason to keep adding cows. Eventually, the pasture is overgrazed and becomes useless for everyone. The same pattern shows up in many modern situations: overfishing in the ocean, traffic on public roads, even air pollution. In each case, individuals acting in their own interest end up harming a resource they all depend on. For many years, economists thought the only solutions were government rules or private ownership. But the political scientist Elinor Ostrom found that many communities manage shared resources successfully on their own, by creating local rules and monitoring each other. Her work earned her a Nobel Prize in 2009.

talk.title: How Birds Navigate
talk.text: How do migrating birds find their way over thousands of kilometers? Researchers have discovered that birds use several tools at once. During the day, many species navigate using the position of the sun. At night, some birds, like the indigo bunting, use the stars. In one famous experiment, young buntings were raised in a planetarium, a building where the night sky is projected onto a ceiling. When the researchers rotated the projected sky, the birds changed the direction they tried to fly. Birds also seem to sense the Earth's magnetic field. Scientists believe that special proteins in birds' eyes may allow them to see magnetic lines. And as they get closer to their destination, birds rely on familiar landmarks, like rivers, coastlines, and mountains, as well as smells. What's remarkable is that birds can switch between these tools depending on the weather. On cloudy nights, when the stars are hidden, they depend more on the magnetic field.

talk.title: Anchoring
talk.text: I'd like to talk about a cognitive bias that affects nearly every negotiation you'll ever take part in: anchoring. Anchoring refers to our tendency to rely too heavily on the first piece of information we receive when making a judgment. In a classic study, participants spun a wheel that was rigged to stop at either ten or sixty-five. They were then asked to estimate the percentage of African countries in the United Nations. Those who'd seen sixty-five gave estimates that were, on average, almost twice as high as those who'd seen ten, even though they knew the number was random. Now, the implications for business are considerable. In salary negotiations, the first figure mentioned tends to shape the entire discussion, which is why some experts advise making the first offer yourself, provided you've done your research. Interestingly, being aware of the bias doesn't eliminate it. Even experienced real estate agents, when given different listing prices for the same house, produced valuations that were pulled toward the listed price, while insisting the price hadn't influenced them.

talk.title: Dating the Past with Tree Rings
talk.text: Today we're going to look at dendrochronology, the science of dating events using tree rings. Most of you know that a tree adds one ring per year. What's less obvious is that the width of each ring reflects the growing conditions that year: wet years produce wide rings, while droughts produce narrow ones. Because trees in the same region experience the same weather, they share a distinctive pattern of wide and narrow rings, a bit like a barcode. Researchers can match the pattern in a living tree with the pattern in an old wooden beam, and then overlap that with even older samples. By chaining samples together in this way, scientists in Europe have built continuous records stretching back more than twelve thousand years. The applications go well beyond biology. Archaeologists have used tree rings to determine exactly when medieval buildings were constructed, and climate scientists use them to reconstruct rainfall patterns from periods long before weather records existed. Tree rings have even helped calibrate radiocarbon dating, correcting errors in that method of up to several centuries.

talk.title: Why We Have Leap Years
talk.text: Have you ever wondered why February sometimes has twenty-nine days? It's because of something called a leap year. The Earth takes about three hundred sixty-five and a quarter days to travel around the sun. But our calendar year has only three hundred sixty-five days. So every year, the calendar falls about six hours behind. After four years, those extra hours add up to almost one full day. To fix this, we add an extra day, February twenty-ninth, every four years. Without leap years, our seasons would slowly move. After a few hundred years, summer would start in what we now call autumn.

talk.title: How Bees Make Honey
talk.text: Today let's talk about how bees make honey. First, worker bees fly from flower to flower and collect a sweet liquid called nectar. They store the nectar in a special stomach and carry it back to the hive. There, they pass the nectar to other bees, who chew it for about half an hour. Then the bees put it into small wax cells. The nectar is still very watery, so the bees fan it with their wings to dry it. When most of the water is gone, the nectar has become honey. Finally, the bees cover each cell with wax to keep the honey clean. One bee makes only about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in its whole life.

talk.title: The Bystander Effect
talk.text: In psychology, the bystander effect refers to a surprising finding: people are less likely to help someone in an emergency when other people are present. You might expect the opposite, that more witnesses would mean more help. But in a series of experiments in the 1960s, researchers found that participants who believed they were the only person hearing someone in distress helped quickly, while those who thought several others could hear often did nothing. Researchers point to two main causes. The first is diffusion of responsibility: when many people are present, each person feels less personally responsible. The second is social influence. In an unclear situation, people look at how others react, and if no one else seems worried, they assume there's no emergency. The good news is that simply knowing about the effect can reduce it. And if you ever need help in a crowd, experts suggest pointing to one specific person and asking them directly.

talk.title: The Columbian Exchange
talk.text: Historians use the term Columbian Exchange to describe the massive transfer of plants, animals, and diseases between the Americas and the rest of the world that followed 1492. Its consequences are difficult to overstate. Crops native to the Americas, such as potatoes, maize, and tomatoes, eventually transformed diets across Europe, Africa, and Asia. The potato, in particular, could produce more calories per acre than traditional European grains, and some scholars argue it contributed substantially to population growth in eighteenth-century Europe. The exchange flowed in the other direction as well. Europeans introduced horses, cattle, and wheat to the Americas, reshaping indigenous economies and ways of life. Horses, for instance, enabled some Plains peoples to adopt a highly mobile, bison-hunting culture. Yet the most devastating consequence was biological. Diseases such as smallpox, to which indigenous populations had no prior exposure, spread with catastrophic speed, killing a large proportion of the population in many regions, often before the newcomers themselves had arrived in those areas.

talk.title: Opportunity Cost
talk.text: One of the most useful concepts in economics is also one of the most frequently misunderstood: opportunity cost. The opportunity cost of a choice isn't the money you spend; it's the value of the best alternative you give up. Suppose you spend a Saturday working a shift that pays a hundred dollars instead of going to a friend's concert. The opportunity cost of working is the concert, and the opportunity cost of the concert is the hundred dollars you'd have earned. This framing has some counterintuitive implications. Consider a student deciding whether to attend graduate school. Tuition is obvious, but the larger cost is often invisible: the salary the student would have earned during those years. Economists argue that ignoring these hidden costs leads people to make decisions that look sensible on paper but aren't. The concept also explains why time becomes more valuable as income rises. A highly paid professional who spends an afternoon repainting her own house may, in economic terms, be paying far more than if she'd hired someone, even though no money changes hands.
